storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — skies are clear, radar is empty and the air is very dry, so the cove gets the same quiet, cool night as the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer in play: the air (61°F) is already about 5°F colder than the Sound (66°F) at 4 PM and falls to roughly 8°F colder by 6 PM, so the Sound isn't changing anything tonight.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a dry northwest flow covers the whole area. The 3:47 PM radar scan shows no storm cells anywhere in range, there are no National Weather Service alerts, and the forecast is simply "Sunny" going to "Clear" overnight.

No fuel for storms: the atmosphere's storm energy (CAPE) is zero now and stays zero through the hours the forecast model covers. Winds aloft are fairly strong — about 40 kt of wind change between the surface and 6 km — but with no instability and very dry air (dew point 37°F at Riverside YC) that produces nothing more than a breeze.

Local effect — not in play: the cove's usual protection comes from a layer of cool, stable air that sits over the Sound when the water is much cooler than the land. Tonight it is the other way round: the water is 66°F and the air is 61°F at 4 PM, a gap of about −5°F against a +5°F threshold for any buffer. The Sound holds its temperature while the air cools after sunset (6:27 PM), so the gap only widens the wrong way — about −6°F at 5 PM and −8°F by 6 PM. There is no sea breeze either; the wind is blowing off the land.

Most likely outcome: a clear, dry, cool evening in the cove and everywhere around it, with temperatures sliding from about 60°F at 5 PM to the mid-50s by 10 PM. No difference between the cove and inland towns.

What would change the call: nothing on the horizon tonight. It would take storm cells appearing on radar to the west or a new NWS alert, and neither is supported by the current dry, stable air mass.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind — northwest off the land, easing to light after sunset; no sea breeze in play

hourly.shift_note: after sunset — gusts fading, holes near shore

wind.tactics_blurb: Northwest wind off the land: puffy and shifty at 6–8 kt early, fading to a patchy 5 kt after sunset. Stay center where the average pressure is best, tack on the headers, and sail to the next puff rather than committing to a side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of wind day: this is a moderate gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day. A sea breeze needs the land to be at least 5°F warmer than the Sound; today the inland air is 61°F against 66°F water — an air–water temperature difference of −5°F — so there is no thermal engine at all. Only 1 of 18 coastal stations shows any southerly flow. The wind is the regional northwest flow: the airports and well-sited stations average 9 kt, and Riverside YC read NW 10 kt gusting 14 (10-minute average 9 kt) at 4 PM.

Will it hold: gradient wind doesn't die with the sun the way a sea breeze does, but tonight's is modest and already easing. Expect about 8 kt gusting 12 at 5 PM, 6 kt around sunset (6:27 PM), then a patchy 5 kt through 10 PM as the land cools and the gusts stop mixing down. It should stay sailable but drifts toward light-air conditions late — the last hours are the ones at risk of holes.

Where the pressure sits: a northwest wind reaches the cove over land, so it arrives in puffs with lulls between them. The best average pressure is usually mid-cove, away from the immediate lee of the trees and houses on the northwest shore; puffs roll down off that shore with holes in between. That argues for the center of the course rather than either edge.

Shift character: oscillating, not persistent — no front or boundary is coming through (pressure is flat around 1018 hPa across the network, and Boston and Groton upstream are also northwest, so there is no backdoor cold front to worry about). Expect swings of 15–20° either side of roughly 305–315°, tied to the puffs. Tack on the headers and keep your head out of the boat looking for the next dark patch. After sunset the oscillations get slower and less regular as the breeze goes light.

Model versus stations: the forecast model (HRRR) has the wind at 283° and 8 kt for 4 PM, while Riverside YC and Bridgeport airport are both further right at 310–315° and a couple of knots stronger. The table follows the stations for direction and nudges the speeds up by 1–2 kt. The model had only reached 6 PM when this was produced, so the 7–10 PM rows lean on the National Weather Service hourly forecast (northwest 5–6 kt) rather than model output.

On the water: 6–8 kt early is pleasant one-design dinghy racing with gains and losses on every shift; by 8 PM it is a 5 kt light-air evening where boat speed in the lulls and connecting the puffs matter more than which side you chose. It is cool, too — upper 50s falling to the mid-50s after dark.

data_caveats: The forecast model (HRRR 3 PM run) had only published through 6 PM at fetch time; the 7–10 PM wind rows are based on the National Weather Service hourly forecast and the evening trend, not model output.

The 5–6 PM wind is nudged 1–2 kt above the model and about 20° further right (more northerly), because Riverside YC and Bridgeport airport were reading stronger and more northwesterly than the model at 4 PM.
The forecast model has no gust data; gust figures are estimates scaled from current Riverside YC gusts.
The marine-layer trend covers only three forecast hours (through 6 PM); it does not affect tonight's call because there is no marine layer and no storms.
Buoy 44040 (western Sound) observation is 75 minutes old and was given little weight in the live wind picture.
Westchester airport (KHPN) wind sensor is down; its temperature is still used as the inland reference.
Wind direction agreement across the station network is low (44%), mostly from sheltered backyard stations reading near calm — typical of a puffy wind off the land rather than a sign of a front.
